prize_parts.citation: For the optical lattice clock: Katori's magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, and Ye's development of it to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18 with many-atom statistical power

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B048 to B013. The chair asked whether I can write a three-person B048 citation that survives the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and 3D topological insulator objections. After a second look I cannot, and I would rather say so than defend it. The HgTe quantum-well experiment was done on the BHZ proposal, Zhang is deceased, and the 3D work (Fu-Kane-Mele, Moore-Balents, Roy, Hsieh-Hasan) is as influential as the 2D case, so any three-name set misstates who found what. The 2016 prize on topological phases also leaves a real question about marginal novelty. This is a judgment about credit, and my view of the physics of B048 is unchanged. On B013 the physics is what I trust most in a result: the magic-wavelength lattice removes the Stark and motional shifts while keeping thousands of atoms in the measurement, and the 10^-18 uncertainty has been checked by independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST), including fibre-linked comparisons. Atomic structure theory has to match experiment in every detail to reach that level, which is the quantitative theory-experiment loop I care about. Katori's concept and Ye's accuracy, stability and many-body clock are separable roles, so two names are defensible. On the chair's first question, the citation should rest on magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms and what it achieved. It should not mention clocks or combs in general, because the 2005 prize covered the comb and the 2012 prize covered single-ion control, and neither covers the lattice concept or the many-atom gain. I also note that I moved because of the credit problem, not because six colleagues prefer B013, and I have tried to test that reasoning myself.
statement.case_against: The reservations I recorded on B013 in round 1 still stand. The prize sits close to 2005 and 2012, and a sceptic can call it a refinement of recognised tools. It is a measurement capability and no new quantum state, and so far no fundamental-physics signal (varying constant, dark-sector coupling) has come from the clocks. The redefinition of the second is pending. Two names leave out Ludlow, Lemke, Hinkley, Bloom, Takamoto, Lemonde, Campbell and others who did hands-on work and the ion-clock lineage, and I cannot weigh these from memory. If an expert review of the earliest lattice-clock proposals shows that someone other than Katori or Ye has priority for the central idea, I would revisit the names. On the broader choice, I still think the committee should give a condensed-matter discovery its due soon, and the clean-credit argument for B013 should not become a standing reason to skip harder cases.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers the Aharonov-Bohm effect and Berry phase (B034) as the unifying root of the topological programmes, and he accepts that the BHZ omission makes B048 fragile, with B048 as his first alternative.
responses.response: I agree that Berry curvature and the Z2 invariant rest on geometric phase, and as a theorist I value that foundation. I cannot support B034 as a prize part, because the credit problems are worse than for B048. Ehrenberg-Siday, Pancharatnam, Mead-Truhlar, Herzberg-Longuet-Higgins and Simon all have priority claims, and Bohm's death means the 1959 effect could be honoured through Aharonov alone. A citation written around two living names would not describe the history accurately. I have dropped B048 as my first choice on the same ground, so I cannot ask him to accept less than I accept myself. My answer to the chair's question for both of us is that neither of us can write a clean citation, and I think we should say that openly. I would welcome his view on whether B048 or B013 is the better fallback in his own judgment, and not only as a concession.

responses.point: Lindroth backs B013 on scientific grounds, citing the magic-wavelength mechanism, reproducibility across independent laboratories and many-body clock physics, and she suggests a citation that mentions fundamental-physics tests and the measurement of time.
responses.response: Her reproducibility argument is the one that moves me, more than the count of supporters. Since she is the atomic physics specialist, I will take her account of the mechanism. I would make one change to her citation. Phrases such as 'opening new possibilities for tests of fundamental physics' promise a payoff that has not yet arrived, and the committee has been careful to avoid that. I would anchor the wording in what has been demonstrated: the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 many-atom result. I also take her point that she cannot reliably weigh the contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto and Hollberg from memory. I share that limit, so an expert check on the earliest lattice-clock proposals before the final ballot seems prudent, as the chair suggested.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice-clock prize is distinct from the comb (2005) and ion-control (2012) prizes because magic-wavelength trapping is a separate concept and the many-atom statistical gain is something ion clocks cannot offer, so the citation must be written around the lattice.
responses.response: I think that is the correct reading, and it answers the novelty objection I raised in round 1 better than I did. The distinction is one of physics. A single trapped ion is limited by its signal-to-noise ratio, while a lattice uses thousands of atoms with the Stark shift cancelled by choice of wavelength, so neither earlier prize implies it. I agree the citation should name the lattice concept and avoid generic wording about clocks. Olsson is right that a comb is a technical foundation of any optical clock, but the same can be said of lasers for many later prizes and it does not make the lattice clock second-order. I also agree with his answer on timing: the prize should recognise demonstrated performance, not the metrological decision on the second.

responses.point: Olsson says the HgTe experiment follows the BHZ proposal whose authors are not credited, that the 2016 prize lowers the novelty margin, and that she would not block B048 but prefers a candidate where proposal and demonstration are both clearly attributed.
responses.response: She is right, and her point is the main reason I have moved. I do not accept that the 2016 prize makes Z2 phases the same discovery, because they are a different symmetry class and need no magnetic field. But a prize that credits the 2007 experiment without the BHZ proposal would describe the history inaccurately. I also note that she moved from B050 to B013 after weighing her own criteria, which I value more than a simple convergence of views. Her remark that two names must be checked against the historical record is where I would put the committee's effort before the final ballot.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from IceCube to B013 and says that he trades some discovery value for clean attribution, and that a third clock-related prize invites a charge of repetition.
responses.response: I respect his candour about trading discovery value for attribution certainty, and I am doing the same, so I do not want to hide it. My view is that B013 does not repeat the earlier prizes if the citation is limited to the lattice concept, and we should put that in the public text. I would also like the committee to remember what we gave up, and I would not call the clock a discovery of a new quantum phenomenon. That is what the topological insulator and IceCube candidates offer, and Danielsson himself knows the IceCube credit problem is not yet resolved. I would keep both on the alternatives list for future cycles.

uncertainties: Whether Katori and Ye are the right two names once an expert has checked the earliest lattice-clock proposals and the roles of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemke, Hinkley and Hollberg. My own knowledge here is second-hand, and I defer to Lindroth and Kroll.
Whether the committee will accept that the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes when the citation is written around magic-wavelength trapping and the many-atom 10^-18 realisation.
Whether waiting for the redefinition of the second, or for a first fundamental-physics result from the clocks, would give a better-timed prize.
Whether my move away from B048 is a sound credit judgment or a reaction to the room. I think it is the former, but I cannot fully exclude the latter.
statement.conflict_note: No change. I have no known personal, institutional or collaborative link to Katori, Ye or the other credited names. My electronic-structure background is closer to B048 and B041 than to atomic clocks, so I defer to Lindroth, Kroll and Johansson on the lattice-clock physics, and I do not regard that proximity as a conflict.
